paras: The killing of Jourique and Sanchez was the fatal shooting of two young Mexican men by Americans in a dispute over land near El Paso, Texas, on or about April 13, 1881. The next evening, while the bodies lay in El Paso awaiting an inquest, a quarrel over the armed Mexicans who had come for them turned into a street shooting in which a policeman and two other men were killed. Wire dispatches carried the two shootings across the United States, often under headlines about wholesale killing in Texas.

A Santa Fe dispatch described two towns facing each other across the river, El Paso and "the town of Franklin (The American El Paso)," and said the killing "created great excitement on both sides of the river."

According to a dispatch from El Paso dated April 15, two young Mexicans named Jourique and Sanchez had been "shot and killed by Americans" two days earlier in "a difficulty about some land" about eight miles up the river. The Santa Fe dispatch placed the killing on "last Wednesday afternoon" and called it a quarrel between "a party of Americans and two Mexicans." A special to the Kansas City Star named the dead men Jilberk Jourique and Jose Sanchez, "two young Mexicans of high standing," and their killers Sam Purdy and Frank Stevenson, adding that the killing "aroused the Mexican residents of the town, who demanded revenge."

The Mexican consul, with an armed force of Mexicans and with the mayor's permission, crossed over and took possession of the bodies. Between five and six o'clock the following evening, as the remains lay in a wagon in front of a justice's office awaiting an inquest, a dispute arose over the armed Mexicans among G. W. Campbell, John Hale and a policeman the papers called Krempkar, Krempken or Kremkaw. Hale covered the policeman with his pistol and shot him, after which the city marshal shot Hale, Campbell and, by accident, a Mexican, leaving "six men lying in the street" at once. Hale died within minutes, the policeman was killed instantly, Campbell died the next morning, and the Mexican was reported in critical condition.

By April 18 the Santa Fe dispatch reported that El Paso and Franklin had been quiet since Thursday. No report of the inquest's verdict, of an arrest of Purdy or Stevenson, or of a trial for either shooting appears in the coverage.

Most papers took the story from the El Paso dispatch distributed through the St. Louis Republican, which ran from April 16 in papers from Maine to Texas and Georgia. Headline writers presented it as Texas lawlessness: "Six Men Shot. The Way they Settle Disputes in Texas Towns" in Portland, "Wholesale Killing in Texas" in Cleveland, Tennessee, and "The Festive El Paso" in Dallas. The Savannah Morning News instead headed it "The Murder of Two Mexicans Followed by a Fatal Fusilade."

The Omaha Bee ran it as "Terrible Vengeance. Mexicans and Americans Slaughtering Each Other," placed El Paso in New Mexico, and asked in a subhead whether the Americans or the "Greasers," an ethnic slur, would be wiped out. Summary columns condensed the story further, the Mineral Point Tribune calling it "a fierce riot" and the Bismarck Tribune placing it at "El Paso, Mexico." None of the versions printed a statement from the consul or the Mexican residents.

Accounts differ on how the street shooting began. A second account printed in the Memphis Appeal and the Chicago Tribune called Hale "a desperado" who tried to intimidate the authorities at the inquest, and said the policeman's shot wounded the newly elected marshal, "Studemire," and killed Hale and a Mexican bystander. The Santa Fe dispatch said the Americans "showed great indignation at the conduct of the Mexicans" and organized a party to attack them, and that Hall shot Kremkaw after mistaking him for a Mexican and was himself shot by an American. The Kansas City special described a "regular pitched battle" in which Hall, Campbell, a man whose name is garbled in print, and a Mexican were killed.
The El Paso dispatch, closest to the scene, counted three dead and the Mexican in critical condition.

reader.title: Killing of Jourique and Sanchez and the El Paso street shooting
bases: Two Mexican men were shot by two named Americans (A2, A3) or 'a party of Americans' (A8) in a quarrel over land (A1, A7), followed the next day by a street gunfight among armed men, a policeman and the marshal while the bodies awaited inquest (A1, A7, A8); no report describes a mob seizing or hunting the victims.

Three independent dispatches, from El Paso via St. Louis (A1, A7), from Kansas City (A2, A3) and from Santa Fe (A8), agree that Americans killed two young Mexicans near El Paso and that a deadly shooting followed while the bodies were in town.

accounts.label: El Paso dispatch (St. Louis Republican wire)
accounts.gist: Two Mexicans killed by Americans in a land difficulty; while the bodies awaited inquest, Hale drew on policeman Krempkar over the armed Mexicans and shot him, and the marshal shot Hale, Campbell and a Mexican by accident.

accounts.label: 'Another account' (desperado version)
accounts.gist: Hale, 'a desperado', tried to intimidate the authorities at the inquest; he and the policeman fired together, the policeman's shot wounding Marshal 'Studemire' and killing Hale and a Mexican bystander, and the marshal mortally wounded Campbell.

accounts.label: Kansas City Star special
accounts.gist: Sam Purdy and Frank Stevenson killed two Mexicans 'of high standing'; Mexican residents demanded revenge, Americans turned out, and a 'pitched battle' killed Hall, Campbell, another man and a Mexican, with the fight 'still going on'.

accounts.label: Santa Fe dispatch
accounts.gist: A party of Americans killed two Mexicans in a quarrel; when armed Mexicans crossed for the bodies, Americans organized to attack them; Hall killed Kremkaw by mistake and was shot by an American; the marshal wounded Campbell and a Mexican fatally; quiet since Thursday.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the El Paso dispatch verbatim under headlines about Texas violence: 'Six Men Shot. The Way they Settle Disputes in Texas Towns', 'Wholesale Shooting in a Texas Town', 'The Festive El Paso'.
The Savannah Morning News headlined 'The Murder of Two Mexicans Followed by a Fatal Fusilade', calling the first killing murder.
The Omaha Bee framed it as ethnic war, 'Terrible Vengeance. Mexicans and Americans Slaughtering Each Other', with a subhead asking whether the Americans or the 'Greasers' would be 'Wiped Out'.
Summary columns condensed it to a quarrel or a 'fierce riot', sometimes misplacing El Paso in Mexico.
